Knowledge takeaway. A coalition can be winning without being minimal; removing redundant members tests how necessary each partner is.

Formal model. Weighted coalition game; enumerate subsets, test threshold and minimality.

N22. Due process, evidence, and right of reply

Problem 231. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 1

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a student may receive a serious penalty only if: (1) at least two independent pieces of evidence support the allegation, and (2) the student is given a chance to respond before the final decision. In a case, one camera record and one independent witness support the allegation, but the student was not allowed to respond.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Camera and witness are independent, so the evidence condition is met. 2. The student was not given a chance to respond. 3. The procedure requires both conditions, so the penalty is not authorized.

Answer. No. The right-to-respond condition is not met.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Problem 232. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 2

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a serious penalty requires two independent pieces of evidence and a chance to respond. In this case there are two friends repeating the same rumor from one original speaker, plus a chance to respond.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails.

Step-by-step solution. 1. The two friends trace to the same original rumor, so they are not two independent pieces under the rule. 2. The response condition is met. 3. Because the evidence condition fails, the serious penalty is not authorized.

Answer. No. The evidence requirement is not met.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Problem 233. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 3

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a student may receive a serious penalty only if: (1) at least two independent pieces of evidence support the allegation, and (2) the student is given a chance to respond before the final decision. In a case, one camera record and one independent witness support the allegation, but the student was not allowed to respond. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Camera and witness are independent, so the evidence condition is met. 2. The student was not given a chance to respond. 3. The procedure requires both conditions, so the penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.

Answer. No. The right-to-respond condition is not met. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Problem 234. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 4

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a serious penalty requires two independent pieces of evidence and a chance to respond. In this case there are two friends repeating the same rumor from one original speaker, plus a chance to respond. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 8 members, requires at least 5 present for quorum, and 8 are present.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. The two friends trace to the same original rumor, so they are not two independent pieces under the rule. 2. The response condition is met. 3. Because the evidence condition fails, the serious penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: compare 8 with 5; 8≥5 is true.

Answer. No. The evidence requirement is not met. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Problem 235. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 5

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a student may receive a serious penalty only if: (1) at least two independent pieces of evidence support the allegation, and (2) the student is given a chance to respond before the final decision. In a case, one camera record and one independent witness support the allegation, but the student was not allowed to respond. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 11 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Camera and witness are independent, so the evidence condition is met. 2. The student was not given a chance to respond. 3. The procedure requires both conditions, so the penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: 11−4=7 independent reports remain.

Answer. No. The right-to-respond condition is not met. Cross-domain answer: 7 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

N23. Samples, surveys, and public opinion

Problem 236. Sampling and opinion: case 1

Knowledge context. Surveys use samples to learn about larger populations. The selection process matters as much as the number of answers.

Given facts. A town wants to estimate how many residents use buses. It surveys only people waiting at the bus station.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. People already at the bus station are more likely than average to use buses. 4. Therefore the method is likely biased.

Answer. Likely biased. People already at the bus station are more likely than average to use buses.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

Problem 237. Sampling and opinion: case 2

Knowledge context. Surveys use samples to learn about larger populations. The selection process matters as much as the number of answers.

Given facts. A school wants opinions on lunch. It randomly selects 10 students from each grade.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. Random selection within every grade gives broad grade coverage; no obvious topic-specific selection is stated. 4. Therefore the method is not obviously biased for the stated target, within the limits given.

Answer. Not obviously biased under the stated design. Random selection within every grade gives broad grade coverage; no obvious topic-specific selection is stated.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. Sports-club members are likely to be more favorable to a sports field than the whole village. 4. Therefore the method is likely biased.

Answer. Likely biased. Sports-club members are likely to be more favorable to a sports field than the whole village.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

Problem 239. Sampling and opinion: case 4

Knowledge context. Surveys use samples to learn about larger populations. The selection process matters as much as the number of answers.

Given facts. A library surveys every 20th visitor entering over a full week.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. Sampling every 20th visitor across a full week is systematic within the visitor population; it may represent visitors reasonably, though not non-visitors. 4. Therefore the method is not obviously biased for the stated target, within the limits given.

Answer. Not obviously biased under the stated design. Sampling every 20th visitor across a full week is systematic within the visitor population; it may represent visitors reasonably, though not non-visitors.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

Problem 240. Sampling and opinion: case 5

Knowledge context. Surveys use samples to learn about larger populations. The selection process matters as much as the number of answers.

Given facts. An online poll is open to anyone who chooses to click it.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. People who choose to click may differ systematically from those who ignore the poll. 4. Therefore the method is likely biased.

Answer. Likely biased. People who choose to click may differ systematically from those who ignore the poll.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

N24. Matching, scheduling, and coverage

Problem 241. Matching people to tasks: case 1

Knowledge context. Scheduling and assignment problems connect people, tasks, times, and constraints.

Given facts. Four students must each receive one different task. Allowed assignments: Ava: ['Map', 'Timeline']; Ben: ['Budget', 'Survey']; Cara: ['Map', 'Survey']; Dion: ['Budget', 'Timeline'].

Rules. Each student gets exactly one allowed task, and each task is used exactly once. A complete assignment must satisfy both conditions.

Task. Find one complete valid assignment. If none exists, explain why.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Start with the most restricted student if one exists. 2. Assign an allowed task, then remove that task from the remaining choices. 3. One complete assignment is {'Ava': 'Map', 'Ben': 'Budget', 'Cara': 'Survey', 'Dion': 'Timeline'}.

Answer. Valid assignment: Ava→Map, Ben→Budget, Cara→Survey, Dion→Timeline.

Knowledge takeaway. A local choice can block a later assignment, so the whole matching must be checked.

Formal model. Bipartite matching / all-different constraint satisfaction.

N25. Meta-reasoning: robustness, information, causality

Problem 246. Meta-reasoning: case 1

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Four equally likely locations A,B,C,D remain possible. Question Q1 asks “Is it A?”; Q2 asks “Is it A or B?” A yes/no question is more balanced when its two answer branches contain more nearly equal numbers of possibilities.

Rules. Use branch sizes as the information criterion in this exercise.

Task. Which question is more balanced and therefore more informative by the stated criterion?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Q1 splits the four possibilities 1 versus 3. 2. Q2 splits them 2 versus 2. 3. The 2–2 split is more balanced.

Answer. Q2.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 247. Meta-reasoning: case 2

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Option A scores between 49 and 53 after measurement error; option B scores between 50 and 52. A ranking is robust only if every allowed value of A remains above every allowed value of B.

Rules. Test worst cases: robust A>B requires min(A)>max(B).

Task. Is the ranking A>B robust?

Step-by-step solution. 1. min(A)=49; max(B)=52. 2. 49>52 is false. 3. Some allowed values reverse the ranking.

Answer. No; the ranking is sensitive to the uncertainty.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 248. Meta-reasoning: case 3

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Claim: “Every town with more roads has shorter average travel time.” Town X has 6 roads and average travel time 35 minutes. Town Y has 4 roads and average travel time 20 minutes.

Rules. A universal claim is disproved by one case that satisfies its condition but not its conclusion.

Task. Do X and Y provide a counterexample to the claim?

Step-by-step solution. 1. X has more roads than Y. 2. Yet X has longer, not shorter, travel time. 3. Therefore the universal claim fails on this pair.

Answer. Yes. X and Y form a counterexample.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 249. Meta-reasoning: case 4

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Across several months, ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Temperature also rises in those months. No intervention is described.

Rules. Correlation between X and Y does not by itself prove X causes Y; a third variable may influence both.

Task. Can we conclude that ice-cream sales cause sunburn?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Sales and sunburn are correlated. 2. Temperature is a plausible common factor stated in the data. 3. Without an intervention or stronger causal evidence, direct causation is not established.

Answer. No. The association alone does not establish that ice-cream sales cause sunburn.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 250. Meta-reasoning: case 5

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Two transport plans are compared. A costs 8, takes 20 minutes, and has safety score 9. B costs 10, takes 25 minutes, and has safety score 9. Lower cost/time and higher safety are better.

Rules. A Pareto-dominates B if A is at least as good on every stated criterion and strictly better on at least one.

Task. Does one plan dominate the other?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A is cheaper than B. 2. A is faster than B. 3. Safety is equal. 4. A is no worse anywhere and better on two criteria.

Answer. A Pareto-dominates B.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

GRADE 2

Difficulty increases through the number of relations and reasoning steps, not through hidden knowledge.

Part A — Foundational reasoning about the world

G1. Positions and orientation

Problem 251. Position chain from Fern to Kite

Knowledge context. A map can be modeled with relative positions. When several moves are given, their effects can be combined rather than memorized as a picture.

Given facts. Cedar is 1 map unit(s) east of Fern; Kite is 1 map unit(s) east of Cedar.

Rules. Treat east as +x, west as −x, north as +y, and south as −y. Add the moves in order. A fact that does not affect any coordinate is irrelevant.

Task. Where is Kite relative to Fern? What is the straight grid displacement measured as |x|+|y|?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Start Fern at (0,0). 2. Translate each relation into a coordinate move. 3. Adding the moves gives (2,0). 4. That coordinate is east of Fern; the grid displacement is |2|+|0|=2.

Answer. Kite is east of Fern; grid displacement 2 unit(s).

Knowledge takeaway. Cardinal directions become easier to reason about when they are treated as relations that can be composed.

Formal model. Grid coordinates; each statement adds a vector; sum the vectors and classify the final coordinate.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Start Zephyr at (0,0). 2. Translate each relation into a coordinate move. 3. Adding the moves gives (0,4). 4. That coordinate is north of Zephyr; the grid displacement is |0|+|4|=4.

Answer. Juniper is north of Zephyr; grid displacement 4 unit(s).

Formal model. Grid coordinates; each statement adds a vector; sum the vectors and classify the final coordinate.

G2. Roads and routes

Problem 256. The best route from Iris to Zephyr

Knowledge context. A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.

Given facts. Iris–Quartz–Zephyr has segment costs [4, 5] (total 9); Iris–Riverbend–Yarrow–Zephyr has segment costs [3, 2, 4] (total 9); Iris–Birch–Zephyr has segment costs [7, 2] (total 9).

Rules. A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.

Task. Which route should a traveler use from Iris to Zephyr, and why?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. All listed routes are open. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 9, on Iris–Quartz–Zephyr.

Answer. Use Iris–Quartz–Zephyr; total cost 9.

Knowledge takeaway. A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.

Formal model. Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

Problem 257. The best route from Iris to Zephyr

Knowledge context. A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.

Given facts. Iris–Riverbend–Zephyr has segment costs [5, 6] (total 11); Iris–Pine–Linden–Zephyr has segment costs [4, 3, 4] (total 11); Iris–Fern–Zephyr has segment costs [8, 3] (total 11).

Rules. A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.

Task. Which route should a traveler use from Iris to Zephyr, and why?

Answer. Use Iris–Riverbend–Zephyr; total cost 11.

Knowledge takeaway. A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.

Formal model. Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

G3. Rivers: upstream and downstream

Problem 261. Following water from North Fork

Knowledge context. River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.

Given facts. North Fork flows into Willow Stream; Blue Creek flows into Willow Stream; Willow Stream flows into Clearwater.

Rules. If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.

Task. Is North Fork upstream of Clearwater? Can water from North Fork reach Clearwater through the stated network?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: North Fork→Willow Stream, Blue Creek→Willow Stream, Willow Stream→Clearwater. 2. Follow arrows starting from North Fork. 3. An arrow path reaches Clearwater, so North Fork is upstream of Clearwater.

Answer. Yes; water from North Fork can reach Clearwater.

Knowledge takeaway. A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.

Formal model. Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.

G4. Neighbours and borders

Problem 266. Crossing the fictional border network of Oak

Knowledge context. Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.

Given facts. Countries are represented by the fictional states Oak, Riverbend, Meadow, Willow, Northfield, Cedar. Shared borders: Oak–Riverbend, Riverbend–Meadow, Meadow–Willow, Oak–Northfield, Northfield–Cedar, Cedar–Willow.

Rules. Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.

Task. What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Oak to Willow? Is Riverbend necessarily crossed?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Oak to Willow. 3. Remove Riverbend and check whether Willow is still reachable from Oak. 4. It is still reachable, so Riverbend is not unavoidable.

Answer. 3 border crossing(s); Riverbend is not unavoidable.

Knowledge takeaway. Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.

Formal model. Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.

G5. Maps, legends, and clues

Problem 271. Reading a layered map legend (A1)

Knowledge context. A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.

Given facts. Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1']. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. A1, B1 Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Map reading often means intersecting clues rather than recognizing one symbol in isolation.

Formal model. Set model; each cell has an attribute set; return cells whose set is a superset of the required set.

G6. Choosing a settlement site

Problem 276. Choosing a safe settlement site: case 1

Knowledge context. Human settlements depend on several factors at once. Some conditions may be compulsory while others are preferences.

Given facts. Candidate sites: Site A: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=2; Site B: water=yes, road=no, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=4; Site C: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=yes, nearby farmland score=4; Site D: water=no, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=6. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 5 cm apart.

Rules. A valid site must have water, road access, and must not be in the flood zone. Among valid sites, choose the one with the highest farmland score. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which site should be selected under the stated mandatory conditions and preference rule? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Separate mandatory conditions from the preference. 2. Filtering by water, road, and flood safety leaves ['Site A']. 3. Compare only the farmland scores of feasible sites: Site A=2. 4. Site A has the best score among valid sites. Cross-domain check: 5×3=15 km.

Answer. Site A. Cross-domain answer: 15 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Good decisions first satisfy hard constraints and only then optimize among the remaining options.

Formal model. Constraint-satisfaction problem followed by a score maximization over feasible options.

G7. Relief and movement cost

Problem 281. Terrain and travel cost from Linden

Knowledge context. Equal-looking distances can require different effort because terrain differs. A simple cost model makes that effect explicit.

Given facts. Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Linden to Stone: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['forest', 'forest', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 9 energy units.

Rules. The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.

Task. Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 9. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.

Answer. Route R1, using 5 energy units.

Knowledge takeaway. Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.

Formal model. Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

G8. Climate from data

Problem 286. Classifying climate data: Station A

Knowledge context. Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.

Given facts. Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=460 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=740 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.

Rules. Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.

Task. Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=460 with 500 mm: it is dry. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.

Answer. Station A is cool and dry; no other station has the same class.

Knowledge takeaway. Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.

Formal model. Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.

G9. Exchange, routes, and capacities

Problem 291. Bottlenecks in the Meadow–Fern exchange network

Knowledge context. Trade and transport networks have capacities. A single narrow connection can limit a much larger network.

Given facts. Goods move from Meadow to Fern along two branches: Meadow→Riverbend capacity 5, Riverbend→Fern capacity 4; Meadow→Cedar capacity 2, Cedar→Fern capacity 6.

Rules. A branch cannot carry more than its smallest edge capacity. Independent branch capacities can be added, but a shared destination capacity can cap the total.

Task. What is the maximum number of units that can reach Fern in one period? Identify the bottleneck(s).

Step-by-step solution. 1. Branch 1 is limited by min(5,4)=4. 2. Branch 2 is limited by min(2,6)=2. 3. Together the branches could carry 6 units. 4. No extra shared cap is given, so the maximum is 6.

Answer. 6 units.

Knowledge takeaway. A bottleneck is a local limit that constrains the total possible flow.

Formal model. Flow network; branch capacity is a minimum along a path; total is the sum of independent branches subject to shared caps.

G10. Regions, sets, and membership

Problem 296. Nested places: Fern, Coastland, and Republic C

Knowledge context. Geography uses nested categories: a locality can be inside a region, a region inside a state, and a state inside a continent.

Given facts. Fern is in Coastland. Coastland is in Republic C. Republic C is in the continent of Meridian.

Rules. If X is contained in Y and Y is contained in Z, then X is contained in Z. The reverse inference is not valid: knowing that two places are in one country does not prove that they are in the same region.

Task. Is Fern in Republic C?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Follow the chain city→region→country. 2. Containment is transitive, so the city is in the country.

Answer. Yes, Fern is in Republic C.

Knowledge takeaway. Hierarchies support upward transitive inference, but they do not justify arbitrary reverse inferences.

Formal model. Containment relation with transitivity; answer membership queries while rejecting invalid converse inference.

Formal model. Containment relation with transitivity; answer membership queries while rejecting invalid converse inference.

H1. Ordering events

Problem 301. Ordering the events of Eastvale

Knowledge context. Historical chronology often starts from partial information: some events are ordered relative to others even when exact dates are not known.

Given facts. Bridge opening happened before Founding. Founding happened before New school. Market charter happened after Bridge opening. Flood happened after New school.

Rules. “Before” is transitive: if A is before B and B is before C, then A is before C. If two events are not connected by the facts, their relative order may be undetermined.

Task. What must be true about the order of Bridge opening and New school? Can the exact order of Market charter and Founding be determined?

Step-by-step solution. 1. From Bridge opening before Founding and Founding before New school, infer Bridge opening before New school. 2. Market charter is only constrained to be after Bridge opening. There is no stated relation between Market charter and Founding. 3. Therefore the first comparison is forced but the second is underdetermined.

Answer. Bridge opening must be before New school. The relative order of Market charter and Founding cannot be determined from the given facts.

Knowledge takeaway. A careful reasoner distinguishes what must be true from what merely could be true.

Formal model. Partial order / directed acyclic graph; use transitive closure and detect incomparable events.

H2. Dates, durations, and centuries

Problem 306. Duration and centuries: 1448–1474

Knowledge context. Dates can be used as numbers, but historical labels such as centuries follow explicit conventions.

Given facts. An institution was founded in 1448 and reorganized in 1474. Use the rule: years 1–100 are the 1st century, 101–200 the 2nd, and so on. Duration is end year minus start year.

Rules. Apply the century rule mechanically; do not infer a century from the first two digits alone. Compute elapsed time by subtraction.

Task. How many years passed between the two events? In which centuries did 1448 and 1474 fall?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Elapsed time: 1474−1448=26 years. 2. Century(1448)=floor((1448−1)/100)+1=15. 3. Century(1474)=15.

Answer. 26 years; 1448 is in the 15th century and 1474 in the 15th century.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronological reasoning combines arithmetic with a naming convention; both should be applied explicitly.

Formal model. Integer arithmetic plus century function c(y)=floor((y−1)/100)+1.

Rules. Apply the century rule mechanically; do not infer a century from the first two digits alone. Compute elapsed time by subtraction.

Task. How many years passed between the two events? In which centuries did 1509 and 1555 fall?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Elapsed time: 1555−1509=46 years. 2. Century(1509)=floor((1509−1)/100)+1=16. 3. Century(1555)=16.

Answer. 46 years; 1509 is in the 16th century and 1555 in the 16th century.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronological reasoning combines arithmetic with a naming convention; both should be applied explicitly.

Formal model. Integer arithmetic plus century function c(y)=floor((y−1)/100)+1.

H3. Sources and supported claims

Problem 311. What can one letter prove?

Knowledge context. Historical sources are evidence, not automatic answers. The strength of a conclusion depends on what the source actually records.

Given facts. A historian has one source: a letter. The source directly shows that a named person wrote a message. A student proposes two claims: C1: a named person wrote a message; C2: the whole population agreed with the ruler.

Rules. A source supports only claims that can reasonably be inferred from what it contains. Absence of evidence for a broad claim is not proof of that claim.

Task. Which claim is directly supported, and which is not justified by this source alone?

Step-by-step solution. 1. The letter directly contains evidence for C1. 2. C2 is much broader and no stated feature of the source measures the opinion of the whole population. 3. Therefore C1 is supported and C2 is not established.

Answer. C1 is supported. C2 is not justified by the source alone.

Knowledge takeaway. Good historical reasoning matches the scope of a claim to the scope of the evidence.

Formal model. Claim-evidence compatibility relation; accept only claims entailed by the source attributes.

H4. Conflicting sources

Problem 316. Resolving conflicting sources: case 1

Knowledge context. Historical accounts can disagree. Reasoning requires evaluating how a source knows what it claims, not simply counting statements.

Given facts. Source A, written on the day of an event, says 40 carts arrived. Source B, copied 80 years later from an unknown account, says 90 carts arrived. Source C is an independent warehouse record from the same week and lists 42 carts. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 3 cm apart.

Rules. When sources conflict, compare proximity to the event, independence, and whether a source has a reason or mechanism to record the specific fact. Agreement between independent relevant sources increases support but does not create absolute certainty. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which account is better supported by the evidence given, and why? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A is contemporary and reports 40. 2. C is an independent operational record and reports 42, close to A. 3. B is much later and has an unknown chain of transmission. 4. The cluster near 40–42 is therefore better supported than 90. Cross-domain check: 3×3=9 km.

Answer. An arrival count near 40–42 carts is better supported than 90. Cross-domain answer: 9 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Independent, relevant, well-positioned evidence usually deserves more weight than late repetition with unknown provenance.

Formal model. Evidence graph with source reliability/independence attributes; compare support for competing hypotheses.

Problem 317. Resolving conflicting sources: case 2

Knowledge context. Historical accounts can disagree. Reasoning requires evaluating how a source knows what it claims, not simply counting statements.

Given facts. Source A, an eyewitness diary, says the bridge opened on Monday. Source B, a later textbook, says Tuesday. Source C, an independent dated toll record, begins charging on Monday. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 33 map sheets and receives 8 additional sheets during the exercise.

Rules. When sources conflict, compare proximity to the event, independence, and whether a source has a reason or mechanism to record the specific fact. Agreement between independent relevant sources increases support but does not create absolute certainty. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Task. Which account is better supported by the evidence given, and why? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A and C are close to the event and independent. 2. Both point to Monday. 3. B is later and conflicts with two stronger, independent pieces of evidence. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00. Mixed-domain verification: 33+8=41.

Answer. Monday is better supported, while remaining a historical conclusion rather than absolute proof. Cross-domain answer: 14:00. Mixed-domain answer: 41 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. Independent, relevant, well-positioned evidence usually deserves more weight than late repetition with unknown provenance.

Formal model. Evidence graph with source reliability/independence attributes; compare support for competing hypotheses.

H5. Causes, conditions, and consequences

Problem 321. Cause-and-consequence chain: case 1

Knowledge context. Many explanations can be represented as condition-and-consequence rules. The logical form matters: necessary, sufficient, AND, and OR are not interchangeable.

Given facts. Facts: Rain occurred; The river was already high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rain and high river satisfy both conditions of the first rule. 2. Infer flooding. 3. Flooding implies road closure. 4. The working siren independently implies a warning. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.

Answer. Flooding, road closure, and a warning can be deduced. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Knowledge takeaway. Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.

Formal model. Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

Problem 322. Cause-and-consequence chain: case 2

Knowledge context. Many explanations can be represented as condition-and-consequence rules. The logical form matters: necessary, sufficient, AND, and OR are not interchangeable.

Given facts. Facts: Rain occurred; The river was not high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 15 members, requires at least 8 present for quorum, and 14 are present.

Rules. Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule. Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rain is true but the high-river condition is false. 2. The AND rule for flooding therefore does not fire. 3. Without flooding, road closure is not inferred. 4. The siren rule still gives a warning. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 8; 14≥8 is true.

Answer. A warning can be deduced, but flooding and road closure cannot be deduced. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.

Formal model. Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 9 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Task. Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Flooding is stated directly, so apply the flooding→road-closure rule. 2. Apply siren→warning. 3. Do not use flooding to infer rain or a high river; that would reverse a rule. Cross-domain check: 9−4=5 independent reports remain.

Answer. Road closure and a warning can be deduced; flooding is already given as a fact. Cross-domain answer: 5 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.

Formal model. Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

H6. Travel through time and space

Problem 326. Courier journey from Stone to Oak

Knowledge context. Historical travel can be analyzed with ordinary distance, speed, and time reasoning when the needed values are supplied.

Given facts. A courier leaves Stone for Oak at 7:00. Distance is 80 km and the stated average speed is 20 km/h. A council meeting in Oak begins at 10.0:00. Ignore stops and use travel time = distance ÷ speed.

Rules. Arrival time equals departure time plus travel time. To attend an event from its beginning, arrival must be no later than the event start.

Task. When does the courier arrive, and can the courier attend the meeting from its beginning?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Travel time=80÷20=4.0 hours. 2. Arrival=7.0+4.0=11.0. 3. Compare 11.0 with meeting time 10.0.

Answer. Arrival at about 11.0:00; no, the meeting has already begun.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronology and geography interact: being able to reach a place in time is a constraint, not a fact to memorize.

Formal model. Arithmetic time model; t_arrive=t_depart+d/v; compare with event time.

H7. Change and continuity

Problem 331. Change and continuity in a settlement: case 1

Knowledge context. History studies both change and continuity. Comparing two snapshots is a systematic way to separate what persisted from what appeared or disappeared.

Given facts. Period 1 features: footpath, market, well, wooden bridge. Period 2 features: market, road, stone bridge, well. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A continuity is a feature present in both periods. A disappearance is present only in Period 1. An appearance is present only in Period 2. A replacement can be described when two differently named features serve the same stated role. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Identify the continuities, disappearances, and appearances. Which conclusions are direct set comparisons rather than interpretations? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Intersection gives continuities: ['market', 'well']. 2. Period1−Period2 gives disappearances: ['footpath', 'wooden bridge']. 3. Period2−Period1 gives appearances: ['road', 'stone bridge']. 4. Only role-based replacement would require extra information; the set comparisons are direct. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. Continuities: ['market', 'well']; disappearances: ['footpath', 'wooden bridge']; appearances: ['road', 'stone bridge']. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Change is not the opposite of continuity; both can occur in the same community at the same time.

Formal model. Set operations: intersection for continuity, set difference for appearance/disappearance.

Task. Identify the continuities, disappearances, and appearances. Which conclusions are direct set comparisons rather than interpretations? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Answer. Continuities: ['market']; disappearances: ['footpath', 'well', 'wooden bridge']; appearances: ['road', 'stone bridge']. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Formal model. Set operations: intersection for continuity, set difference for appearance/disappearance.

H8. Layers and dating objects

Problem 336. Reading an archaeological sequence: case 1

Knowledge context. Archaeological layers provide relative chronological information. Dates from objects add constraints but do not automatically make every date exact.

Given facts. An undisturbed archaeological site has four layers from top to bottom: A, B, C, D. In an undisturbed sequence, lower layers were deposited earlier. D contains an object dated 1300, C contains one dated 1450, and B contains one dated 1600. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 2 cm apart.

Rules. In an undisturbed sequence, a lower layer is older than a layer above it. A securely dated object provides a constraint on the layer that contains it, but one object does not date every other object exactly. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which is older, Layer C or Layer B? Can the exact year of deposition of Layer A be deduced? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. C lies below B, so C is older than B by the stratigraphic rule. 2. No exact dated object or deposition year is given for A. 3. Therefore only relative ordering, not an exact year for A, is justified. Cross-domain check: 2×3=6 km.

Answer. Layer C is older than Layer B. The exact deposition year of Layer A cannot be deduced. Cross-domain answer: 6 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Relative dating and absolute dating answer different questions and should not be confused.

Formal model. Partial order from vertical position plus numeric constraints from dated objects.

C1. Rules and exceptions

Problem 341. Applying a rule with an exception: Ivy

Knowledge context. Rules often have conditions and exceptions. Logical reading prevents us from applying a general rule when an overriding exception is active.

Given facts. Ivy is 11 years old. A library rule says: a child may enter the archive room if age ≥ 12 AND an adult permit is present. Exception: during an evacuation drill, nobody may enter. Permit present: yes. Evacuation drill: no.

Rules. Check exceptions first if they override the general rule. Otherwise every condition joined by AND must be true.

Task. May Ivy enter the archive room under these facts? Show which conditions succeed or fail.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Age test: 11≥12 is False. 2. Permit test is True. 3. Because the general rule uses AND, both tests must pass. 4. Therefore entry is not allowed.

Answer. No, Ivy may not enter.

Knowledge takeaway. The order of reasoning matters when exceptions override ordinary rules.

Formal model. Boolean rule with priority: exception predicate first, then conjunction of eligibility conditions.

C2. Rights as limits on decisions

Problem 346. Majority rule and a protected right: case 1

Knowledge context. Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.

Given facts. A council of 19 members votes 14 to 5 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to speak at a peaceful meeting. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.

Rules. A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.

Task. Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Vote check: 14>5, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (speak at a peaceful meeting) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.

Answer. It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.

Knowledge takeaway. A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.

Formal model. Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.

C3. Voting, majority, and quorum

Problem 351. Quorum and majority in a 19-member committee

Knowledge context. Voting rules often contain more than one threshold. Quorum concerns participation; majority concerns the votes cast according to the stated rule.

Given facts. A committee has 19 members. 19 are present. Votes: yes=9, no=9, abstain=1. Rule: quorum is at least 60% of all members; if quorum exists, a motion passes when yes votes are strictly more than no votes.

Rules. First test quorum using all members as the denominator. Only then compare yes and no; abstentions count for presence but not as no votes under this rule.

Task. Is quorum met, and does the motion pass?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Quorum threshold=ceil(0.60×19)=12. 2. Present=19, so quorum is met. 3. Yes=9, no=9; yes>no is False. 4. Combine the two tests.

Answer. Quorum is met; the motion does not pass.

Knowledge takeaway. Procedural reasoning requires applying tests in the right order and using the correct denominator.

Formal model. Threshold predicates: quorum(present,total) and majority(yes,no); pass = quorum ∧ majority.

C4. Representation and seats

Problem 356. Representing three districts: case 1

Knowledge context. Representation can be modeled by rules that convert population into seats. Different allocation rules can produce different results, so the rule must be stated.

Given facts. Three districts have populations A=120, B=100, C=60. They must share 12 seats. Use this stated method: compute each exact quota population/total×seats; give each district the whole-number part; assign remaining seats to the largest fractional remainders.

Rules. Use only the stated largest-remainder method. Seat totals must add exactly to the available number.

Task. How many seats does each district receive?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Total population=280. 2. Exact quotas: A=5.14, B=4.29, C=2.57. 3. Initial whole seats: [5, 4, 2], leaving 1. 4. Give the remaining seat(s) to the largest remainder(s). 5. Final allocation=[5, 4, 3], which sums to 12.

Answer. A=5, B=4, C=3 seats.

Knowledge takeaway. Fair representation is not just arithmetic; it depends on an explicit apportionment procedure.

Formal model. Largest-remainder apportionment: quotas, floors, then rank fractional remainders.

Problem 360. Representing three districts: case 5

Knowledge context. Representation can be modeled by rules that convert population into seats. Different allocation rules can produce different results, so the rule must be stated.

Given facts. Three districts have populations A=200, B=100, C=120. They must share 12 seats. Use this stated method: compute each exact quota population/total×seats; give each district the whole-number part; assign remaining seats to the largest fractional remainders.

Rules. Use only the stated largest-remainder method. Seat totals must add exactly to the available number.

Task. How many seats does each district receive?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Total population=420. 2. Exact quotas: A=5.71, B=2.86, C=3.43. 3. Initial whole seats: [5, 2, 3], leaving 2. 4. Give the remaining seat(s) to the largest remainder(s). 5. Final allocation=[6, 3, 3], which sums to 12.

Answer. A=6, B=3, C=3 seats.

Knowledge takeaway. Fair representation is not just arithmetic; it depends on an explicit apportionment procedure.

Formal model. Largest-remainder apportionment: quotas, floors, then rank fractional remainders.

C5. Institutions and roles

Problem 361. Which institution has the role? Repair a broken public road

Knowledge context. Civic institutions divide responsibilities. A problem can be solved by matching an action to a clearly defined function.

Given facts. Roles are defined as follows: Town Council makes local policy and approves the budget; Public Works Office maintains roads; Local Court decides legal disputes; Election Committee administers elections; School Board sets school policies. A resident asks which institution should repair a broken public road.

Rules. Match the requested action to the stated role. Do not choose an institution merely because it is powerful or familiar.

Task. Should the request go first to the Public Works Office or the Health Office? Why?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the action: repair a broken public road. 2. Find the role whose definition contains that function: Public Works Office. 3. Health Office has a different stated role, so it is not the first match.

Answer. The request should go first to the Public Works Office.

Knowledge takeaway. Institutional reasoning is role matching, not guessing which body is “most important.”

Formal model. Bipartite relation between actions and authorized institutional roles.

C6. Public budgets and priorities

Problem 366. Choosing a public budget package: case 1

Knowledge context. Public budgets require choices under limited resources. A transparent model separates costs, benefits, and mandatory obligations.

Given facts. A town has a budget of 14 units. Projects (cost, benefit): park=(4,5); bridge repair=(6,9); library books=(3,4); drainage=(5,8). Cross-domain check: a local committee has 14 members, requires at least 8 present for quorum, and 14 are present.

Rules. Choose a subset whose total cost does not exceed the budget. Maximize total benefit. If a mandatory project is stated, every feasible plan must include it. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Which set of projects gives the greatest total benefit while satisfying every constraint? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Budget limit is 14. 2. Evaluate feasible combinations (and keep the mandatory project if any). 3. The best feasible combination has cost 14 and benefit 21: ['bridge repair', 'library books', 'drainage']. 4. No higher-benefit feasible combination exists under the stated costs. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 8; 14≥8 is true.

Answer. Choose bridge repair, library books, drainage; cost 14, benefit 21. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. Optimization means comparing feasible alternatives under an explicit objective, not simply choosing the cheapest item.

Formal model. 0/1 knapsack with optional mandatory-item constraint; maximize benefit subject to total cost ≤ budget.

Task. Which set of projects gives the greatest total benefit while satisfying every constraint? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Budget limit is 15. 2. Evaluate feasible combinations (and keep the mandatory project if any). 3. The best feasible combination has cost 14 and benefit 21: ['bridge repair', 'library books', 'drainage']. 4. No higher-benefit feasible combination exists under the stated costs. Cross-domain check: 13−4=9 independent reports remain.

Answer. Choose bridge repair, library books, drainage; cost 14, benefit 21. Cross-domain answer: 9 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Optimization means comparing feasible alternatives under an explicit objective, not simply choosing the cheapest item.

Formal model. 0/1 knapsack with optional mandatory-item constraint; maximize benefit subject to total cost ≤ budget.

C7. Collective choice and preferences

Problem 371. Pairwise collective choice: Park versus Library

Knowledge context. Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.

Given facts. Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 4 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 5 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 2 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.

Rules. For a pairwise contest, count how many voters prefer each of the two options. Ignore the third option for that comparison.

Task. In a pairwise vote between Park and Library, which option wins?

Step-by-step solution. 1. For each group, check whether Park or Library is ranked higher. 2. Totals: Park=6, Library=5. 3. Therefore the result is Park.

Answer. Park wins 6 to 5.

Knowledge takeaway. A collective decision rule must be explicit; different rules can summarize the same rankings differently.

Formal model. Preference rankings; for pair (a,b), sum weights of voters ranking a>b versus b>a.

Part B — New and mixed reasoning domains

N1. Scale, proportion, and distance

Problem 376. Map scale 1:10000

Knowledge context. Map scale links a model to the real world through proportional reasoning.

Given facts. A map has scale 1:10000. The measured map distance between two points is 4 cm. Rule: 1 cm on the map represents 10000 cm in reality; 100,000 cm = 1 km.

Rules. Multiply map length by the scale denominator, then convert units. A scale is a ratio, not an added distance.

Task. What is the real straight-line distance in kilometres?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Real centimetres=4×10000=40000. 2. Convert to kilometres: 40000÷100,000=0.4.

Answer. 0.4 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Scale problems are ratio problems: keep units explicit and conversion becomes mechanical.

Formal model. Proportion d_real=d_map×denominator, followed by unit conversion.

N2. Coordinates and constraint-based location

Problem 381. Locating a point by constraints: case 1

Knowledge context. Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.

Given facts. A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 6. It satisfies x+y=4 and x−y=0.

Rules. A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.

Task. Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List pairs satisfying x+y=4. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=0. 3. The remaining set is [(2, 2)].

Answer. P=(2, 2); the solution is unique.

Knowledge takeaway. A constraint problem is solved by satisfying all conditions together, not one at a time independently.

Formal model. Constraint satisfaction over integer pairs (x,y).

N3. Earth, Sun, seasons, and local time

Problem 386. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 1

Knowledge context. Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.

Given facts. For this classroom model, Eastport is 1 time zone(s) east of Westport. Each zone east is one hour later. At Westport it is 10:00.

Rules. Moving east adds one hour per stated time zone; moving west subtracts. Use the given model only.

Task. What local time is it in Eastport?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Time difference is +1 hour(s) because Eastport is east. 2. 10+1=11 (mod 24).

Answer. 11:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

Problem 389. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 4

Given facts. Use this simplified model: Earth’s axis is tilted. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are generally longer around June than around December. Compare June and December for the same place. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. Use the stated seasonal relation; do not infer daily weather from season. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Which of the two months has the longer daylight period in this model, and can that fact alone tell us whether it will rain? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.

Answer. June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced. Cross-domain check: compare 11 with 6; 11≥6 is true.

Answer. June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

N4. Stocks, flows, and conservation

Problem 391. Reservoir stock and flow: case 1

Knowledge context. Many geographic and civic quantities are stocks and flows: water in a reservoir, people in a city, or goods in a warehouse.

Given facts. A reservoir starts with 30 water units. Each day 5 units flow in and 5 units flow out. Assume these rates stay constant for 4 days.

Rules. Stock at the end = starting stock + total inflow − total outflow. Flow is an amount per time period; stock is the amount currently stored.

Task. How much water is stored after 4 days? Is the stock increasing or decreasing each day?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Daily net change=5−5=0. 2. Over 4 days, net change=4×0=0. 3. End stock=30+(0)=30.

Answer. 30 units; the stock is unchanged.

Knowledge takeaway. Do not confuse a stored amount with a rate of change; conservation links them.

Formal model. Difference equation S(t+1)=S(t)+inflow−outflow.

N5. Density, capacity, and crowding

Problem 396. Density and capacity in a public space: case 1

Knowledge context. Density compares an amount with the space available. It can reveal crowding even when two places have similar total populations.

Given facts. A park zone covers 4 hectares and currently has 30 visitors. For this exercise, comfortable density is at most 7 visitors per hectare.

Rules. Density = number ÷ area. A zone exceeds comfortable capacity if density is greater than the stated threshold.

Task. What is the visitor density, and is the zone above the stated comfortable capacity?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Density=30÷4=7.50 visitors/hectare. 2. Compare 7.50 with the threshold 7.

Answer. 7.50 visitors/hectare; above capacity.

Knowledge takeaway. Totals and densities answer different questions; always identify the denominator.

Formal model. Ratio density=N/A followed by threshold comparison.

N6. Land use and spatial compatibility

Problem 401. Land-use compatibility on four plots: case 1

Knowledge context. Land-use planning combines spatial relationships with compatibility rules.

Given facts. Four plots lie in a line A–B–C–D. Assign one different use to each plot: school, factory, park, homes. Constraints: the factory may not be adjacent to the school; the park must be adjacent to the homes. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. An assignment is valid only if every use is placed exactly once and all adjacency constraints hold. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Give one valid assignment and explain why it satisfies every constraint. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Try the assignment A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory. 2. Factory and school are not adjacent. 3. Park and homes are adjacent. 4. Each use appears exactly once. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.

Answer. A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory is a valid assignment. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A place can be unsuitable not because of its own properties, but because of what would be next to it.

Formal model. Permutation CSP with all-different and adjacency/non-adjacency constraints.

N7. Natural risk: hazard, exposure, protection

Problem 406. Hazard, exposure, and protection: case 1

Knowledge context. Natural risk depends on more than the physical hazard. Exposure and protective measures also affect outcomes.

Given facts. For this classroom model, risk index = hazard × exposure ÷ protection. Data: Site A: hazard=2, exposure=4, protection=1; Site B: hazard=4, exposure=2, protection=2; Site C: hazard=3, exposure=3, protection=2.

Rules. Use the formula exactly as stated. A higher hazard does not necessarily mean higher risk if exposure or protection differs.

Task. Compute the risk index for each site. Which site has the lowest modeled risk?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compute hazard×exposure÷protection for each site. 2. Results: A=8.00, B=4.00, C=4.50. 3. The lowest value is Site B.

Answer. A=8.00; B=4.00; C=4.50. Lowest: Site B.

Knowledge takeaway. Separating hazard from risk prevents the mistaken idea that the most dangerous process always creates the greatest overall risk.

Formal model. Explicit risk-index function over three variables; compare computed values.

N8. Ecosystems and indirect effects

Problem 411. Indirect effects in a food chain: case 1

Knowledge context. Ecosystems contain dependency networks. A change at one point can propagate indirectly through several links.

Given facts. Food relation: rabbit eats grass; fox eats rabbit; eagle eats fox. Classroom rule: if a food source sharply decreases and no alternative food is given, the consumer may also decrease. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. Follow dependency arrows from food to consumer. The rule supports possible directional effects, not exact population numbers. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. If rabbit sharply decreases, which later populations may be indirectly affected according to the rule? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. fox depends directly on rabbit, so it may decrease. 2. eagle depends on fox, so it may also be indirectly affected. 3. grass is food for rabbit; the stated rule does not imply it decreases for the same reason. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. fox may decrease directly and eagle may be affected indirectly. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Indirect effects require following the direction of dependency and respecting the limits of the stated model.

Formal model. Directed dependency graph; propagate a qualitative decrease along outgoing dependency links.

Formal model. Directed dependency graph; propagate a qualitative decrease along outgoing dependency links.

N9. Renewable resources and sustainable use

Problem 416. Regeneration and harvest: case 1

Knowledge context. Renewable does not mean unlimited. A resource can decline when use exceeds regeneration.

Given facts. A forest resource starts at 120 units. Each year it regenerates 12 units and people harvest 10 units. Assume these amounts stay constant for 3 years and no other changes occur.

Rules. Annual net change = regeneration − harvest. In this simplified model, use is sustainable over the period if stock does not decline.

Task. What is the stock after 3 years, and is the harvest sustainable under this classroom definition?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Annual net change=12−10=2. 2. Three-year change=6. 3. Final stock=120+(6)=126. 4. Compare final stock with starting stock.

Answer. 126 units; sustainable under the stated definition.

Knowledge takeaway. Sustainability is a balance between renewal and extraction over time.

Formal model. Stock-flow model with regeneration and harvest; test non-decreasing stock.

Problem 419. Regeneration and harvest: case 4

Knowledge context. Renewable does not mean unlimited. A resource can decline when use exceeds regeneration.

Given facts. A forest resource starts at 120 units. Each year it regenerates 18 units and people harvest 19 units. Assume these amounts stay constant for 3 years and no other changes occur.

Rules. Annual net change = regeneration − harvest. In this simplified model, use is sustainable over the period if stock does not decline.

Task. What is the stock after 3 years, and is the harvest sustainable under this classroom definition?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Annual net change=18−19=-1. 2. Three-year change=-3. 3. Final stock=120+(-3)=117. 4. Compare final stock with starting stock.

Answer. 117 units; not sustainable under the stated definition.

Knowledge takeaway. Sustainability is a balance between renewal and extraction over time.

Formal model. Stock-flow model with regeneration and harvest; test non-decreasing stock.

N10. Migration and population balance

Problem 421. Population balance in a town: case 1

Knowledge context. Population changes through births, deaths, immigration, and emigration.

Given facts. A town begins the year with 1200 residents. During the year: births=20, deaths=12, people moving in=34, people moving out=25.

Rules. End population = start + births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. Natural change and migration change are separate components.

Task. Compute natural change, migration change, and the year-end population.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Natural change=20−12=8. 2. Migration change=34−25=9. 3. Total change=8+9=17. 4. End population=1200+17=1217.

Answer. Natural change +8; migration change +9; end population 1217.

Knowledge takeaway. Breaking total change into components helps explain why a population grew or shrank.

Formal model. Balance equation P1=P0+births−deaths+in−out.

N11. Time intervals and overlapping events

Problem 426. Overlapping historical intervals: case 1

Knowledge context. Historical periods often overlap rather than forming a single neat sequence.

Given facts. Event A lasted from year 100 to 140. Event B lasted from 100 to 131. Treat intervals as continuous for this exercise.

Rules. Two intervals overlap when max(start times) < min(end times). Overlap length = min(end times) − max(start times), if positive.

Task. Did the events overlap? If so, for how many years?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Later start=max(100,100)=100. 2. Earlier end=min(140,131)=131. 3. Difference=131−100=31.

Answer. Yes, overlap 31 years.

Knowledge takeaway. Interval reasoning distinguishes “before/after” from “overlapping in time.”

Formal model. Interval intersection; compute max starts and min ends.

N12. Genealogy and generations

Problem 431. Reasoning across generations: case 1

Knowledge context. Genealogies are relational graphs. Generation distance can be counted through parent links.

Given facts. Maya is a parent of Noah. Noah is a parent of Lina. Maya is also a parent of Owen. Owen is a parent of Sara. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A parent is one generation above a child. A grandparent is two parent-links above. People who share a parent are siblings under this simplified model. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. What family relation between Maya and Lina follows from the stated links? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Maya→Noah is one parent link. 2. Noah→Lina is a second parent link. 3. Two links give the grandparent relation. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. Maya is a grandparent of Lina. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Family relations can be derived step by step from a small set of explicit links.

Formal model. Directed parent graph; kinship predicates derived from path length and shared ancestors.

Task. What family relation between Noah and Lina follows from the stated links? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. The relation is stated directly. Cross-domain check: 7×4=28 km.

Formal model. Directed parent graph; kinship predicates derived from path length and shared ancestors.

N13. Anachronisms and temporal compatibility

Problem 436. Temporal compatibility in a story set in 1400

Knowledge context. Anachronism can be tested as a compatibility problem when the relevant date ranges are supplied.

Given facts. For this problem, availability intervals are: Technology A: 1200–1600; Institution B: 1500–1900; Tool C: 1700–2000; Practice D: 1300–1450. A story is set in 1400 and mentions Technology A and Tool C together. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 4 cm apart.

Rules. An item is temporally compatible with a year only if the year lies inside its stated availability interval. An anachronism is an item placed outside its given interval. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which mentioned item, if any, is anachronistic in the story? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Check 1400 against Technology A interval 1200–1600. 2. Check 1400 against Tool C interval 1700–2000. 3. Items outside their intervals: ['Tool C']. Cross-domain check: 4×3=12 km.

Answer. Anachronistic: Tool C. Cross-domain answer: 12 km.

Knowledge takeaway. The reasoning does not require memorizing invention dates if the intervals are part of the problem.

Formal model. Interval membership test for each object-event pair.
