Problem 624. Pairwise collective choice: Library versus Park

Knowledge context. Group preferences can be aggregated in different ways. Pairwise majority asks a specific question about two options at a time.

Given facts. Three public projects are considered: Park, Library, Sports Hall. Voter groups and rankings: 7 voters rank Park>Library>Sports Hall; 6 voters rank Library>Sports Hall>Park; 5 voters rank Sports Hall>Park>Library. Use pairwise majority: compare two options at a time; each voter supports the one ranked higher.

Rules. For a pairwise contest, count how many voters prefer each of the two options. Ignore the third option for that comparison.

Task. In a pairwise vote between Library and Park, which option wins?

Step-by-step solution. 1. For each group, check whether Library or Park is ranked higher. 2. Totals: Library=6, Park=12. 3. Therefore the result is Park.

Answer. Park wins 12 to 6.

Knowledge takeaway. A collective decision rule must be explicit; different rules can summarize the same rankings differently.

Formal model. Preference rankings; for pair (a,b), sum weights of voters ranking a>b versus b>a.

Part B — New and mixed reasoning domains

N1. Scale, proportion, and distance

Problem 626. Map scale 1:10000

Knowledge context. Map scale links a model to the real world through proportional reasoning.

Given facts. A map has scale 1:10000. The measured map distance between two points is 5 cm. Rule: 1 cm on the map represents 10000 cm in reality; 100,000 cm = 1 km.

Rules. Multiply map length by the scale denominator, then convert units. A scale is a ratio, not an added distance.

Task. What is the real straight-line distance in kilometres?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Real centimetres=5×10000=50000. 2. Convert to kilometres: 50000÷100,000=0.5.

Answer. 0.5 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Scale problems are ratio problems: keep units explicit and conversion becomes mechanical.

Formal model. Proportion d_real=d_map×denominator, followed by unit conversion.

N2. Coordinates and constraint-based location

Problem 631. Locating a point by constraints: case 1

Knowledge context. Coordinates turn location into numbers. Multiple spatial clues can be treated as simultaneous constraints.

Given facts. A point P lies on an integer grid with x,y from 0 to 7. It satisfies x+y=6 and x−y=0. It also satisfies x≥2.

Rules. A location is valid only if it satisfies every stated equation and inequality at the same time.

Task. Which coordinate(s) can P occupy? Is the solution unique?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List pairs satisfying x+y=6. 2. Keep only those also satisfying x−y=0. 3. The remaining set is [(3, 3)].

Answer. P=(3, 3); the solution is unique.

Knowledge takeaway. A constraint problem is solved by satisfying all conditions together, not one at a time independently.

Formal model. Constraint satisfaction over integer pairs (x,y).

N3. Earth, Sun, seasons, and local time

Problem 636. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 1

Knowledge context. Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.

Given facts. For this classroom model, Eastport is 1 time zone(s) east of Westport. Each zone east is one hour later. At Westport it is 11:00.

Rules. Moving east adds one hour per stated time zone; moving west subtracts. Use the given model only.

Task. What local time is it in Eastport?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Time difference is +1 hour(s) because Eastport is east. 2. 11+1=12 (mod 24).

Answer. 12:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

Problem 639. Earth, sunlight, and local time: case 4

Knowledge context. Earth–Sun relationships explain broad patterns such as day length and local time, but a problem should state the simplified model it expects children to use.

Given facts. Use this simplified model: Earth’s axis is tilted. In the Northern Hemisphere, days are generally longer around June than around December. Compare June and December for the same place. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 15 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. Use the stated seasonal relation; do not infer daily weather from season. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Which of the two months has the longer daylight period in this model, and can that fact alone tell us whether it will rain? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced. Cross-domain check: 15−4=11 independent reports remain.

Answer. June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone. Cross-domain answer: 11 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

Task. Which of the two months has the longer daylight period in this model, and can that fact alone tell us whether it will rain? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Apply the stated tilt-season relation. 2. June has the longer daylight period in the Northern Hemisphere. 3. The rule contains no information about rainfall, so rainfall cannot be deduced. Cross-domain check: 5×2=10 km.

Answer. June has longer daylight; rainfall cannot be determined from this fact alone. Cross-domain answer: 10 km.

Knowledge takeaway. A model supports only the conclusions encoded in its rules; seasonal light does not automatically determine daily weather.

Formal model. Rule-based astronomical/time-zone model; apply signed offsets or seasonal relation.

N4. Stocks, flows, and conservation

Problem 641. Reservoir stock and flow: case 1

Knowledge context. Many geographic and civic quantities are stocks and flows: water in a reservoir, people in a city, or goods in a warehouse.

Given facts. A reservoir starts with 35 water units. Each day 5 units flow in and 6 units flow out. Assume these rates stay constant for 5 days.

Rules. Stock at the end = starting stock + total inflow − total outflow. Flow is an amount per time period; stock is the amount currently stored.

Task. How much water is stored after 5 days? Is the stock increasing or decreasing each day?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Daily net change=5−6=-1. 2. Over 5 days, net change=5×-1=-5. 3. End stock=35+(-5)=30.

Answer. 30 units; the stock is decreasing.

Knowledge takeaway. Do not confuse a stored amount with a rate of change; conservation links them.

Formal model. Difference equation S(t+1)=S(t)+inflow−outflow.

Formal model. Difference equation S(t+1)=S(t)+inflow−outflow.

N5. Density, capacity, and crowding

Problem 646. Density and capacity in a public space: case 1

Knowledge context. Density compares an amount with the space available. It can reveal crowding even when two places have similar total populations.

Given facts. A park zone covers 4 hectares and currently has 35 visitors. For this exercise, comfortable density is at most 8 visitors per hectare.

Rules. Density = number ÷ area. A zone exceeds comfortable capacity if density is greater than the stated threshold.

Task. What is the visitor density, and is the zone above the stated comfortable capacity?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Density=35÷4=8.75 visitors/hectare. 2. Compare 8.75 with the threshold 8.

Answer. 8.75 visitors/hectare; above capacity.

Knowledge takeaway. Totals and densities answer different questions; always identify the denominator.

Formal model. Ratio density=N/A followed by threshold comparison.

N6. Land use and spatial compatibility

Problem 651. Land-use compatibility on four plots: case 1

Knowledge context. Land-use planning combines spatial relationships with compatibility rules.

Given facts. Four plots lie in a line A–B–C–D. Assign one different use to each plot: school, factory, park, homes. Constraints: the factory may not be adjacent to the school; the park must be adjacent to the homes. The school must be on an end plot.

Rules. An assignment is valid only if every use is placed exactly once and all adjacency constraints hold.

Task. Give one valid assignment and explain why it satisfies every constraint.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Try the assignment A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory. 2. Factory and school are not adjacent. 3. Park and homes are adjacent. The school is on an end plot. 4. Each use appears exactly once.

Answer. A=school, B=park, C=homes, D=factory is a valid assignment.

Knowledge takeaway. A place can be unsuitable not because of its own properties, but because of what would be next to it.

Formal model. Permutation CSP with all-different and adjacency/non-adjacency constraints.

N7. Natural risk: hazard, exposure, protection

Problem 656. Hazard, exposure, and protection: case 1

Knowledge context. Natural risk depends on more than the physical hazard. Exposure and protective measures also affect outcomes.

Given facts. For this classroom model, risk index = hazard × exposure ÷ protection. Data: Site A: hazard=2, exposure=4, protection=1; Site B: hazard=4, exposure=2, protection=2; Site C: hazard=4, exposure=3, protection=2.

Rules. Use the formula exactly as stated. A higher hazard does not necessarily mean higher risk if exposure or protection differs.

Task. Compute the risk index for each site. Which site has the lowest modeled risk?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compute hazard×exposure÷protection for each site. 2. Results: A=8.00, B=4.00, C=6.00. 3. The lowest value is Site B.

Answer. A=8.00; B=4.00; C=6.00. Lowest: Site B.

Knowledge takeaway. Separating hazard from risk prevents the mistaken idea that the most dangerous process always creates the greatest overall risk.

Formal model. Explicit risk-index function over three variables; compare computed values.

N8. Ecosystems and indirect effects

Problem 661. Indirect effects in a food chain: case 1

Knowledge context. Ecosystems contain dependency networks. A change at one point can propagate indirectly through several links.

Given facts. Food relation: rabbit eats grass; fox eats rabbit; eagle eats fox. Classroom rule: if a food source sharply decreases and no alternative food is given, the consumer may also decrease. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 68 map sheets and receives 2 additional sheets during the exercise.

Rules. Follow dependency arrows from food to consumer. The rule supports possible directional effects, not exact population numbers. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Task. If rabbit sharply decreases, which later populations may be indirectly affected according to the rule? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. fox depends directly on rabbit, so it may decrease. 2. eagle depends on fox, so it may also be indirectly affected. 3. grass is food for rabbit; the stated rule does not imply it decreases for the same reason. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00. Mixed-domain verification: 68+2=70.

Answer. fox may decrease directly and eagle may be affected indirectly. Cross-domain answer: 14:00. Mixed-domain answer: 70 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. Indirect effects require following the direction of dependency and respecting the limits of the stated model.

Formal model. Directed dependency graph; propagate a qualitative decrease along outgoing dependency links.

Knowledge takeaway. Indirect effects require following the direction of dependency and respecting the limits of the stated model.

Formal model. Directed dependency graph; propagate a qualitative decrease along outgoing dependency links.

N9. Renewable resources and sustainable use

Problem 666. Regeneration and harvest: case 1

Knowledge context. Renewable does not mean unlimited. A resource can decline when use exceeds regeneration.

Given facts. A forest resource starts at 130 units. Each year it regenerates 12 units and people harvest 11 units. Assume these amounts stay constant for 3 years and no other changes occur.

Rules. Annual net change = regeneration − harvest. In this simplified model, use is sustainable over the period if stock does not decline.

Task. What is the stock after 3 years, and is the harvest sustainable under this classroom definition?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Annual net change=12−11=1. 2. Three-year change=3. 3. Final stock=130+(3)=133. 4. Compare final stock with starting stock.

Answer. 133 units; sustainable under the stated definition.

Knowledge takeaway. Sustainability is a balance between renewal and extraction over time.

Formal model. Stock-flow model with regeneration and harvest; test non-decreasing stock.

N10. Migration and population balance

Problem 671. Population balance in a town: case 1

Knowledge context. Population changes through births, deaths, immigration, and emigration.

Given facts. A town begins the year with 1300 residents. During the year: births=20, deaths=13, people moving in=36, people moving out=25.

Rules. End population = start + births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration. Natural change and migration change are separate components.

Task. Compute natural change, migration change, and the year-end population.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Natural change=20−13=7. 2. Migration change=36−25=11. 3. Total change=7+11=18. 4. End population=1300+18=1318.

Answer. Natural change +7; migration change +11; end population 1318.

Knowledge takeaway. Breaking total change into components helps explain why a population grew or shrank.

Formal model. Balance equation P1=P0+births−deaths+in−out.

N11. Time intervals and overlapping events

Problem 676. Overlapping historical intervals: case 1

Knowledge context. Historical periods often overlap rather than forming a single neat sequence.

Given facts. Event A lasted from year 100 to 145. Event B lasted from 100 to 134. Treat intervals as continuous for this exercise.

Rules. Two intervals overlap when max(start times) < min(end times). Overlap length = min(end times) − max(start times), if positive.

Task. Did the events overlap? If so, for how many years?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Later start=max(100,100)=100. 2. Earlier end=min(145,134)=134. 3. Difference=134−100=34.

Answer. Yes, overlap 34 years.

Knowledge takeaway. Interval reasoning distinguishes “before/after” from “overlapping in time.”

Formal model. Interval intersection; compute max starts and min ends.

N12. Genealogy and generations

Problem 681. Reasoning across generations: case 1

Knowledge context. Genealogies are relational graphs. Generation distance can be counted through parent links.

Given facts. Maya is a parent of Noah. Noah is a parent of Lina. Maya is also a parent of Owen. Owen is a parent of Sara. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. A parent is one generation above a child. A grandparent is two parent-links above. People who share a parent are siblings under this simplified model. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. What family relation between Maya and Lina follows from the stated links? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Maya→Noah is one parent link. 2. Noah→Lina is a second parent link. 3. Two links give the grandparent relation. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.

Answer. Maya is a grandparent of Lina. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Knowledge takeaway. Family relations can be derived step by step from a small set of explicit links.

Formal model. Directed parent graph; kinship predicates derived from path length and shared ancestors.

N13. Anachronisms and temporal compatibility

Problem 686. Temporal compatibility in a story set in 1400

N14. Provenance and chain of custody

Problem 691. Provenance and chain of custody: case 1

Knowledge context. Provenance records where an object came from and how it moved between custodians.

Given facts. An artifact record states: found by Excavator on day 1; transferred to Museum A on day 2; sent from Museum A to Research Lab on day 5; returned by Research Lab to Museum B on day 8. Every transfer must name both sender and receiver. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A continuous chain of custody requires each handoff to connect the previous holder to the next. A missing sender or receiver creates a gap that limits certainty about continuous custody. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Is the stated chain of custody complete under the rule? If not, identify the gap. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Read the transfers in time order. 2. Check that every transfer links the previous holder to the next. 3. Every handoff names both sides and connects continuously. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. The chain is complete under the stated rule. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A strong provenance claim depends on an unbroken sequence of documented handoffs.

Formal model. Time-ordered path through holders; verify continuity of sender/receiver pairs.

N15. Perspective, interest, and source credibility

Problem 696. Perspective, interest, and source quality: case 1

Knowledge context. Sources have perspectives and interests. Credibility is not a simple label; it depends on the claim being evaluated and how the source could know it.

Given facts. Three sources describe a proposed market tax. Source A is a merchant who would pay the tax and argues it is harmful. Source B is a council report that estimates revenue and lists its calculation. Source C is a traveler repeating a rumor heard in another town. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 5 cm apart.

Rules. Perspective and interest do not automatically make a source false. Evaluate relevance, access to information, explicit evidence, and independence. A source with an interest may still provide useful facts, but its claims should be checked. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which source is best positioned to estimate the amount of revenue, and which source should be treated most cautiously for that numerical claim? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Revenue estimation requires access to tax rates and expected transactions. 2. Source B explicitly provides a calculation and is directly about the policy. 3. Source C is a secondhand rumor from elsewhere and has the weakest access to the specific numerical question. 4. Source A has an interest, but interest alone is not enough to discard it. Cross-domain check: 5×3=15 km.

Answer. Source B is best positioned for the revenue estimate; Source C should be treated most cautiously for that numerical claim. Cross-domain answer: 15 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Bias is a reason to inspect evidence, not a magic switch that makes every statement true or false.

Formal model. Source-claim assessment using access, relevance, independence, and evidentiary support.

N16. Uncertain data, intervals, and limits

Problem 701. Reasoning with uncertain intervals: case 1

Knowledge context. Measurements and historical dates can be uncertain. An interval represents a range of possibilities rather than one exact number.

Given facts. Two measurements are uncertain intervals. A is between 8 and 12. B is between 13 and 17. A statement “A is definitely greater than B” is valid only if A’s minimum is greater than B’s maximum.

Rules. For a definite comparison under interval uncertainty, test the worst cases. Overlapping intervals usually prevent a strict guaranteed ordering.

Task. Can we conclude that A is definitely greater than B? What comparison is justified?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A minimum=8, maximum=12; B minimum=13, maximum=17. 2. Test A_min > B_max: 8>17 is False. 3. If false, at least one allowed pair of values defeats the “definitely greater” claim.

Answer. No. The intervals do not justify saying A is definitely greater than B.

Knowledge takeaway. Robust conclusions must remain true across all values allowed by the uncertainty.

Formal model. Interval arithmetic / worst-case comparison.

N17. Counterfactual reasoning

Problem 706. Counterfactual intervention: close the gate

Knowledge context. Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Given facts. Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 12 members, requires at least 7 present for quorum, and 11 are present.

Rules. A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Under the intervention “close the gate”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Actual chain gives high river, then flood, then market closure. 2. Intervene: set gate=closed. 3. The flood rule requires an unclosed gate, so flooding no longer follows. 4. Without flooding, market closure does not follow. Cross-domain check: compare 11 with 7; 11≥7 is true.

Answer. With the gate closed, the model no longer implies flooding or market closure. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.

Formal model. Structural causal rules with a do-style intervention on one variable.

Problem 707. Counterfactual intervention: remove heavy rain

Knowledge context. Counterfactual reasoning asks what the model predicts if one condition were changed while the rest of the causal structure is held fixed.

Given facts. Causal rules for a simplified town model: heavy rain → high river; high river AND unclosed gate → flooded square; flooded square → market closes. Actual facts: heavy rain occurred and the gate was not closed. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 13 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Under the intervention “remove heavy rain”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Intervene: heavy rain=false. 2. Then high river is not generated by the first rule. 3. Without high river, flooding and market closure are not generated. Cross-domain check: 13−4=9 independent reports remain.

Answer. Without heavy rain, the model generates neither high river, flood, nor market closure. Cross-domain answer: 9 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.

Formal model. Structural causal rules with a do-style intervention on one variable.

Rules. A counterfactual intervention changes one specified fact and then recomputes consequences from the rules. Keep all other stated rules the same unless the intervention changes them. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Under the intervention “keep gate open”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Gate already remains open. 2. Heavy rain gives high river. 3. High river plus open gate gives flood, then market closure. Cross-domain check: 3×5=15 km.

Answer. The original chain remains: flood and market closure occur. Cross-domain answer: 15 km.

Knowledge takeaway. A counterfactual is not ordinary storytelling; it is a controlled change followed by recomputation.

Formal model. Structural causal rules with a do-style intervention on one variable.

Task. Under the intervention “prevent high river”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Intervene directly: high river=false. 2. Even with rain, the counterfactual intervention fixes high river as prevented for this question. 3. Flood requires high river, so it does not follow. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.

Answer. Preventing the high river blocks the flood and market closure in this model. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.

Task. Under the intervention “keep market open”, what changes in the consequences? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

N18. Public goods and common contributions

Problem 711. Funding a shared public project: case 1

Knowledge context. Public goods can benefit many people at once, which creates coordination problems about contributions.

Given facts. A community project is built only if total voluntary contributions reach 14 tokens. Contributions from 7 households are [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3]. Everyone can use the project if it is built, including households that contribute zero.

Rules. Add contributions and compare with the threshold. A public-good threshold concerns whether the project is produced; it does not by itself decide whether every contribution pattern is fair.

Task. Is the project built? How many additional tokens, if any, are needed?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Total contribution=1+2+3+4+1+2+3=16. 2. Compare 16 with threshold 14. 3. Additional amount needed=max(0,14−16)=0.

Answer. The project is built. Additional tokens needed: 0.

Knowledge takeaway. Threshold provision and fairness are separate questions; first determine whether enough resources exist.

Formal model. Sum contributions; compare with provision threshold; compute shortfall.

N19. Common resources and avoiding depletion

Problem 716. Using a shared renewable resource: case 1

Knowledge context. A common resource can be overused when many individually reasonable withdrawals add up to more than regeneration.

Given facts. A shared fishery has 90 fish at the start of the period and regenerates 10. There are 6 users, each planning to take 3. For this simplified exercise, the stock should not decline below its starting level if use is to be called non-depleting.

Rules. End stock = start + regeneration − total harvest. Total harvest is number of users × harvest per user.

Task. What is the end stock? Is the planned use non-depleting under the stated definition? What equal per-user harvest would exactly match regeneration?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Total harvest=6×3=18. 2. End stock=90+10−18=82. 3. To match regeneration exactly, equal harvest per user would be 10÷6=1.67.

Answer. End stock 82; depleting. Equal regeneration-matching share: 1.67 each.

Knowledge takeaway. The shared-resource problem appears at the total level, so individual plans must be aggregated.

Formal model. Commons stock equation plus equal-share benchmark.

N20. Fairness: equal, proportional, and need-based

Problem 721. Fair allocation by the rule: equal

Knowledge context. Fairness is not one formula. Equal shares, proportional shares, and need-based shares embody different principles.

Given facts. A relief fund has 45 units for three districts A, B, C. Populations are [10, 20, 30]; need scores are [1, 5, 3]. Three fairness principles are defined: equal = same amount each; population-proportional = shares in ratio 10:20:30; need-proportional = shares in ratio 1:5:3.

Rules. Different fairness principles answer different questions. Apply the principle named in the task; do not mix them unless asked to compare.

Task. Allocate the fund equally.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Equal share=45÷3=15.00. 2. Allocation result: A=15.00, B=15.00, C=15.00.

Answer. A=15.00, B=15.00, C=15.00.

Knowledge takeaway. A sound argument states the fairness rule first and then applies it consistently.

Formal model. Allocation function parameterized by a fairness principle and weights.

Formal model. Allocation function parameterized by a fairness principle and weights.

N21. Negotiation, coalitions, and agreement

Problem 726. Coalition formation: case 1

Knowledge context. In representative bodies, groups may need to cooperate to reach a decision threshold.

Given facts. Three groups have seats A=7, B=3, C=3. A governing coalition needs at least 7 seats. Any two groups may cooperate.

Rules. A coalition is winning if the sum of its members’ seats reaches the threshold. Minimal winning means it is winning but removing any member makes it lose.

Task. Which coalitions are minimal winning coalitions?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Majority threshold=7. 2. Add seats for each possible coalition. 3. Minimal winning coalitions: [('A', 7)].

Answer. A with 7 seats.

Knowledge takeaway. A coalition can be winning without being minimal; removing redundant members tests how necessary each partner is.

Formal model. Weighted coalition game; enumerate subsets, test threshold and minimality.

N22. Due process, evidence, and right of reply

Problem 731. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 1

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a student may receive a serious penalty only if: (1) at least two independent pieces of evidence support the allegation, and (2) the student is given a chance to respond before the final decision. In a case, one camera record and one independent witness support the allegation, but the student was not allowed to respond. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Camera and witness are independent, so the evidence condition is met. 2. The student was not given a chance to respond. 3. The procedure requires both conditions, so the penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. No. The right-to-respond condition is not met. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Problem 732. Procedure, evidence, and a right to respond: case 2

Knowledge context. Fair procedures often combine evidentiary standards with an opportunity for the affected person to answer the case.

Given facts. A school rule says a serious penalty requires two independent pieces of evidence and a chance to respond. In this case there are two friends repeating the same rumor from one original speaker, plus a chance to respond. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 4 km and two checkpoints are 6 cm apart.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. The two friends trace to the same original rumor, so they are not two independent pieces under the rule. 2. The response condition is met. 3. Because the evidence condition fails, the serious penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: 6×4=24 km.

Answer. No. The evidence requirement is not met. Cross-domain answer: 24 km.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Rules. Independence concerns distinct information sources, not merely the number of people repeating one source. Every required procedural condition must be satisfied. Task. May the serious penalty be imposed under the stated procedure? Identify the condition that succeeds or fails. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Camera and witness are independent, so the evidence condition is met. 2. The student was not given a chance to respond. 3. The procedure requires both conditions, so the penalty is not authorized. Cross-domain check: 11−4=7 independent reports remain. Mixed-domain verification: 75+6=81.

Answer. No. The right-to-respond condition is not met. Cross-domain answer: 7 independent reports. Mixed-domain answer: 81 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. A correct outcome does not excuse skipping a required procedure when the rule explicitly makes procedure part of validity.

Formal model. Conjunctive procedural predicate over evidence independence/count and response opportunity.

N23. Samples, surveys, and public opinion

Problem 736. Sampling and opinion: case 1

Knowledge context. Surveys use samples to learn about larger populations. The selection process matters as much as the number of answers.

Given facts. A town wants to estimate how many residents use buses. It surveys only people waiting at the bus station. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 3 cm apart.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias. Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. People already at the bus station are more likely than average to use buses. 4. Therefore the method is likely biased. Cross-domain check: 3×3=9 km.

Answer. Likely biased. People already at the bus station are more likely than average to use buses. Cross-domain answer: 9 km.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

Problem 737. Sampling and opinion: case 2

Given facts. A school wants opinions on lunch. It randomly selects 10 students from each grade. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. A sample is more representative when selection does not systematically favor people connected to the answer. Random or broad systematic sampling can reduce selection bias; voluntary or topic-specific locations may create bias. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Is the sampling method likely to be biased for the stated question? Explain the direction of the possible bias. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Identify the target population. 2. Compare the selection method with that target. 3. Random selection within every grade gives broad grade coverage; no obvious topic-specific selection is stated. 4. Therefore the method is not obviously biased for the stated target, within the limits given. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00.

Answer. Not obviously biased under the stated design. Random selection within every grade gives broad grade coverage; no obvious topic-specific selection is stated. Cross-domain answer: 10:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A large biased sample can still give a misleading estimate; representativeness is a reasoning question about selection.

Formal model. Sampling-frame analysis: compare inclusion mechanism with target population and likely outcome-related selection.

N24. Matching, scheduling, and coverage

Problem 741. Matching people to tasks: case 1

Knowledge context. Scheduling and assignment problems connect people, tasks, times, and constraints.

Given facts. Four students must each receive one different task. Allowed assignments: Ava: ['Map', 'Timeline']; Ben: ['Budget', 'Survey']; Cara: ['Map', 'Survey']; Dion: ['Budget', 'Timeline']. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 76 map sheets and receives 2 additional sheets during the exercise.

Rules. Each student gets exactly one allowed task, and each task is used exactly once. A complete assignment must satisfy both conditions. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Task. Find one complete valid assignment. If none exists, explain why. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Start with the most restricted student if one exists. 2. Assign an allowed task, then remove that task from the remaining choices. 3. One complete assignment is {'Ava': 'Map', 'Ben': 'Budget', 'Cara': 'Survey', 'Dion': 'Timeline'}. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00. Mixed-domain verification: 76+2=78.

Answer. Valid assignment: Ava→Map, Ben→Budget, Cara→Survey, Dion→Timeline. Cross-domain answer: 14:00. Mixed-domain answer: 78 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. A local choice can block a later assignment, so the whole matching must be checked.

Formal model. Bipartite matching / all-different constraint satisfaction.

N25. Meta-reasoning: robustness, information, causality

Problem 746. Meta-reasoning: case 1

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Four equally likely locations A,B,C,D remain possible. Question Q1 asks “Is it A?”; Q2 asks “Is it A or B?” A yes/no question is more balanced when its two answer branches contain more nearly equal numbers of possibilities. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 16 members, requires at least 9 present for quorum, and 14 are present.

Rules. Use branch sizes as the information criterion in this exercise. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Which question is more balanced and therefore more informative by the stated criterion? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Q1 splits the four possibilities 1 versus 3. 2. Q2 splits them 2 versus 2. 3. The 2–2 split is more balanced. Cross-domain check: compare 14 with 9; 14≥9 is true.

Answer. Q2. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 747. Meta-reasoning: case 2

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Option A scores between 49 and 53 after measurement error; option B scores between 50 and 52. A ranking is robust only if every allowed value of A remains above every allowed value of B. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 13 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. Test worst cases: robust A>B requires min(A)>max(B). For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Is the ranking A>B robust? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. min(A)=49; max(B)=52. 2. 49>52 is false. 3. Some allowed values reverse the ranking. Cross-domain check: 13−4=9 independent reports remain.

Answer. No; the ranking is sensitive to the uncertainty. Cross-domain answer: 9 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 748. Meta-reasoning: case 3

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Claim: “Every town with more roads has shorter average travel time.” Town X has 6 roads and average travel time 35 minutes. Town Y has 4 roads and average travel time 20 minutes. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 5 km and two checkpoints are 8 cm apart.

Rules. A universal claim is disproved by one case that satisfies its condition but not its conclusion. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Do X and Y provide a counterexample to the claim? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. X has more roads than Y. 2. Yet X has longer, not shorter, travel time. 3. Therefore the universal claim fails on this pair. Cross-domain check: 8×5=40 km.

Answer. Yes. X and Y form a counterexample. Cross-domain answer: 40 km.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 749. Meta-reasoning: case 4

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Across several months, ice-cream sales and sunburn cases rise together. Temperature also rises in those months. No intervention is described. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. Correlation between X and Y does not by itself prove X causes Y; a third variable may influence both. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Can we conclude that ice-cream sales cause sunburn? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Sales and sunburn are correlated. 2. Temperature is a plausible common factor stated in the data. 3. Without an intervention or stronger causal evidence, direct causation is not established. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.

Answer. No. The association alone does not establish that ice-cream sales cause sunburn. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

Problem 750. Meta-reasoning: case 5

Knowledge context. Good reasoning includes checking how informative, robust, falsifiable, causal, or dominated a conclusion is.

Given facts. Two transport plans are compared. A costs 8, takes 20 minutes, and has safety score 9. B costs 10, takes 25 minutes, and has safety score 9. Lower cost/time and higher safety are better. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 11 members, requires at least 6 present for quorum, and 11 are present.

Rules. A Pareto-dominates B if A is at least as good on every stated criterion and strictly better on at least one. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Does one plan dominate the other? Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A is cheaper than B. 2. A is faster than B. 3. Safety is equal. 4. A is no worse anywhere and better on two criteria. Cross-domain check: compare 11 with 6; 11≥6 is true.

Answer. A Pareto-dominates B. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. A result can be numerically correct yet epistemically weak; meta-reasoning evaluates the quality of the inference itself.

Formal model. Meta-level predicate over hypotheses or decisions: information balance, robustness, counterexample, causality, or dominance.

GRADE 4

Difficulty increases through the number of relations and reasoning steps, not through hidden knowledge.

Part A — Foundational reasoning about the world

G1. Positions and orientation

Problem 751. Position chain from Fern to Alder

Knowledge context. A map can be modeled with relative positions. When several moves are given, their effects can be combined rather than memorized as a picture.

Given facts. Meadow is 1 map unit(s) east of Fern; Alder is 1 map unit(s) east of Meadow. A museum in Meadow opens on Saturday.

Rules. Treat east as +x, west as −x, north as +y, and south as −y. Add the moves in order. A fact that does not affect any coordinate is irrelevant.

Task. Where is Alder relative to Fern? What is the straight grid displacement measured as |x|+|y|? Identify any irrelevant fact.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Start Fern at (0,0). 2. Translate each relation into a coordinate move. 3. Adding the moves gives (2,0). 4. That coordinate is east of Fern; the grid displacement is |2|+|0|=2. 5. The museum sentence changes no coordinate, so it is a distractor.

Answer. Alder is east of Fern; grid displacement 2 unit(s). The museum fact is irrelevant.

Knowledge takeaway. Cardinal directions become easier to reason about when they are treated as relations that can be composed.

Formal model. Grid coordinates; each statement adds a vector; sum the vectors and classify the final coordinate.

G2. Roads and routes

Problem 756. The best route from Elm to Willow

Knowledge context. A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.

Given facts. Elm–Northfield–Willow has segment costs [6, 7] (total 13); Elm–Riverbend–Harbor–Willow has segment costs [5, 2, 6] (total 13); Elm–Birch–Willow has segment costs [9, 4] (total 13).

Rules. A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.

Task. Which route should a traveler use from Elm to Willow, and why?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. All listed routes are open. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 13, on Elm–Northfield–Willow.

Answer. Use Elm–Northfield–Willow; total cost 13.

Knowledge takeaway. A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.

Formal model. Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

Problem 757. The best route from Oak to Grove

Knowledge context. A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.

Given facts. Oak–Dover–Grove has segment costs [7, 8] (total 15); Oak–Fern–Juniper–Grove has segment costs [6, 3, 6] (total 15); Oak–Riverbend–Grove has segment costs [10, 5] (total 15). The road Oak–Fern is closed.

Rules. A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.

Task. Which route should a traveler use from Oak to Grove, and why?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. Remove any route containing a closed road. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 15, on Oak–Dover–Grove.

Answer. Use Oak–Dover–Grove; total cost 15.

Knowledge takeaway. A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.

Formal model. Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

Problem 759. The best route from Harbor to Meadow

Knowledge context. A road map can be modeled as a graph. The best route depends on the stated criterion, not on how short it looks on paper.

Given facts. Harbor–Riverbend–Meadow has segment costs [9, 10] (total 19); Harbor–Iris–Yarrow–Meadow has segment costs [8, 5, 6] (total 19); Harbor–Oak–Meadow has segment costs [12, 7] (total 19). The road Harbor–Iris is closed.

Rules. A route is feasible only if all of its roads are open. The cost of a route is the sum of its segment costs. Choose the feasible route with the smallest total.

Task. Which route should a traveler use from Harbor to Meadow, and why?

Step-by-step solution. 1. List the candidate routes and their segment costs. 2. Remove any route containing a closed road. 3. Add the segment costs for every feasible route. 4. The smallest feasible total is 19, on Harbor–Riverbend–Meadow.

Answer. Use Harbor–Riverbend–Meadow; total cost 19.

Knowledge takeaway. A shortest path is a reasoning result: first respect constraints, then compare the remaining costs.

Formal model. Weighted graph; delete forbidden edges; minimize the sum of edge weights.

G3. Rivers: upstream and downstream

Problem 761. Following water from Silver River

Knowledge context. River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.

Given facts. Silver River flows into Blue Creek; Clearwater flows into Blue Creek; Blue Creek flows into Meadow River. A canal diverts some water from Clearwater to a reservoir, but the remaining flow still reaches Blue Creek.

Rules. If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.

Task. Is Silver River upstream of Meadow River? Can water from Silver River reach Meadow River through the stated network?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: Silver River→Blue Creek, Clearwater→Blue Creek, Blue Creek→Meadow River. 2. Follow arrows starting from Silver River. 3. An arrow path reaches Meadow River, so Silver River is upstream of Meadow River.

Answer. Yes; water from Silver River can reach Meadow River.

Knowledge takeaway. A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.

Formal model. Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.

G4. Neighbours and borders

Problem 766. Crossing the fictional border network of Quartz

Knowledge context. Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.

Given facts. Countries are represented by the fictional states Quartz, Grove, Harbor, Juniper, Fern, Linden. Shared borders: Quartz–Grove, Grove–Harbor, Harbor–Juniper, Quartz–Fern, Fern–Linden, Linden–Juniper.

Rules. Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.

Task. What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Quartz to Juniper? Is Grove necessarily crossed?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Quartz to Juniper. 3. Remove Grove and check whether Juniper is still reachable from Quartz. 4. It is still reachable, so Grove is not unavoidable.

Answer. 3 border crossing(s); Grove is not unavoidable.

Knowledge takeaway. Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.

Formal model. Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.

G5. Maps, legends, and clues

Problem 771. Reading a layered map legend (A1)

Knowledge context. A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.

Given facts. Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 79 map sheets and receives 2 additional sheets during the exercise.

Rules. A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Task. Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1']. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain. Mixed-domain verification: 79+2=81.

Answer. A1, B1 Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports. Mixed-domain answer: 81 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. Map reading often means intersecting clues rather than recognizing one symbol in isolation.

Formal model. Set model; each cell has an attribute set; return cells whose set is a superset of the required set.

G6. Choosing a settlement site

Problem 776. Choosing a safe settlement site: case 1

Knowledge context. Human settlements depend on several factors at once. Some conditions may be compulsory while others are preferences.

Given facts. Candidate sites: Site A: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=2; Site B: water=yes, road=no, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=4; Site C: water=yes, road=yes, flood-zone=yes, nearby farmland score=4; Site D: water=no, road=yes, flood-zone=no, nearby farmland score=6. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 8 cm apart.

Rules. A valid site must have water, road access, and must not be in the flood zone. Among valid sites, choose the one with the highest farmland score. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which site should be selected under the stated mandatory conditions and preference rule? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Separate mandatory conditions from the preference. 2. Filtering by water, road, and flood safety leaves ['Site A']. 3. Compare only the farmland scores of feasible sites: Site A=2. 4. Site A has the best score among valid sites. Cross-domain check: 8×3=24 km.

Answer. Site A. Cross-domain answer: 24 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Good decisions first satisfy hard constraints and only then optimize among the remaining options.

Formal model. Constraint-satisfaction problem followed by a score maximization over feasible options.

G7. Relief and movement cost

Problem 781. Terrain and travel cost from Quartz

Knowledge context. Equal-looking distances can require different effort because terrain differs. A simple cost model makes that effect explicit.

Given facts. Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Quartz to Linden: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['forest', 'forest', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 11 energy units.

Rules. The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.

Task. Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 11. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.

Answer. Route R1, using 5 energy units.

Knowledge takeaway. Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.

Formal model. Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

Problem 782. Terrain and travel cost from Cedar

Knowledge context. Equal-looking distances can require different effort because terrain differs. A simple cost model makes that effect explicit.

Given facts. Terrain energy costs per segment: {'plain': 1, 'forest': 2, 'hill': 3, 'marsh': 4}. Three routes from Cedar to Dover: R1=['plain', 'hill', 'plain']; R2=['plain', 'forest', 'plain', 'plain']; R3=['plain', 'marsh']. The traveler can spend at most 11 energy units.

Rules. The energy of a route is the sum of its terrain costs. A route above the energy limit is infeasible. Among feasible routes, minimize energy.

Task. Which route is feasible and uses the least energy?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compute route totals: R1=5, R2=5, R3=5. 2. Discard any total above 11. 3. The smallest remaining total is R1=5.

Answer. Route R1, using 5 energy units.

Knowledge takeaway. Relief changes the cost of movement; “shortest” and “easiest” are not automatically the same.

Formal model. Weighted paths with a feasibility budget; sum costs and choose the minimum feasible path.

G8. Climate from data

Problem 786. Classifying climate data: Station A

Knowledge context. Climate descriptions summarize long-term patterns. In a reasoning problem, explicit thresholds let us classify numerical data without hidden knowledge.

Given facts. Use this classroom classification: cool if mean temperature <12°C; mild if 12–17°C; warm if >17°C. Dry if annual precipitation <500 mm; wet if ≥500 mm. Data: Station A: T=8°C, P=520 mm; Station B: T=16°C, P=780 mm; Station C: T=12°C, P=520 mm.

Rules. Apply only the stated thresholds. Temperature and precipitation are separate dimensions, so each station receives two labels.

Task. Classify Station A. Then identify whether any other station has the same two-label class.

Step-by-step solution. 1. Compare T=8 with the temperature thresholds: it is cool. 2. Compare P=520 with 500 mm: it is wet. 3. Compare the combined label with the other stations; matches: none.

Answer. Station A is cool and wet; no other station has the same class.

Knowledge takeaway. Classification is the application of clear predicates to data; the rule must be stated before the label is inferred.

Formal model. Numeric predicates with thresholds; output the conjunction of the temperature and precipitation categories.

G9. Exchange, routes, and capacities

Problem 791. Bottlenecks in the Willow–Northfield exchange network

Knowledge context. Trade and transport networks have capacities. A single narrow connection can limit a much larger network.

Given facts. Goods move from Willow to Northfield along two branches: Willow→Iris capacity 7, Iris→Northfield capacity 6; Willow→Oak capacity 2, Oak→Northfield capacity 8. The final warehouse at Northfield can accept at most 10 units.

Rules. A branch cannot carry more than its smallest edge capacity. Independent branch capacities can be added, but a shared destination capacity can cap the total.

Task. What is the maximum number of units that can reach Northfield in one period? Identify the bottleneck(s).

Step-by-step solution. 1. Branch 1 is limited by min(7,6)=6. 2. Branch 2 is limited by min(2,8)=2. 3. Together the branches could carry 8 units. 4. The destination accepts at most 10, so the final maximum is min(8,10)=8.

Answer. 8 units.

Knowledge takeaway. A bottleneck is a local limit that constrains the total possible flow.

Formal model. Flow network; branch capacity is a minimum along a path; total is the sum of independent branches subject to shared caps.

G10. Regions, sets, and membership

Problem 796. Nested places: Birch, Eastvale, and Republic B

Knowledge context. Geography uses nested categories: a locality can be inside a region, a region inside a state, and a state inside a continent.

Given facts. Birch is in Eastvale. Eastvale is in Republic B. Republic B is in the continent of Meridian. Another city, Alder, is also in Republic B, but its region is not specified.

Rules. If X is contained in Y and Y is contained in Z, then X is contained in Z. The reverse inference is not valid: knowing that two places are in one country does not prove that they are in the same region.

Task. Is Birch in Republic B?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Follow the chain city→region→country. 2. Containment is transitive, so the city is in the country.

Answer. Yes, Birch is in Republic B.

Knowledge takeaway. Hierarchies support upward transitive inference, but they do not justify arbitrary reverse inferences.

Formal model. Containment relation with transitivity; answer membership queries while rejecting invalid converse inference.

Formal model. Containment relation with transitivity; answer membership queries while rejecting invalid converse inference.

H1. Ordering events

Problem 801. Ordering the events of Green Valley

Knowledge context. Historical chronology often starts from partial information: some events are ordered relative to others even when exact dates are not known.

Given facts. Founding happened before New school. New school happened before Flood. Bridge opening happened after Founding. Market charter happened after Flood.

Rules. “Before” is transitive: if A is before B and B is before C, then A is before C. If two events are not connected by the facts, their relative order may be undetermined.

Task. What must be true about the order of Founding and Flood? Can the exact order of Bridge opening and New school be determined?

Step-by-step solution. 1. From Founding before New school and New school before Flood, infer Founding before Flood. 2. Bridge opening is only constrained to be after Founding. There is no stated relation between Bridge opening and New school. 3. Therefore the first comparison is forced but the second is underdetermined.

Answer. Founding must be before Flood. The relative order of Bridge opening and New school cannot be determined from the given facts.

Knowledge takeaway. A careful reasoner distinguishes what must be true from what merely could be true.

Formal model. Partial order / directed acyclic graph; use transitive closure and detect incomparable events.

H2. Dates, durations, and centuries

Problem 806. Duration and centuries: 1699–1731

Knowledge context. Dates can be used as numbers, but historical labels such as centuries follow explicit conventions.

Given facts. An institution was founded in 1699 and reorganized in 1731. Use the rule: years 1–100 are the 1st century, 101–200 the 2nd, and so on. Duration is end year minus start year.

Rules. Apply the century rule mechanically; do not infer a century from the first two digits alone. Compute elapsed time by subtraction.

Task. How many years passed between the two events? In which centuries did 1699 and 1731 fall?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Elapsed time: 1731−1699=32 years. 2. Century(1699)=floor((1699−1)/100)+1=17. 3. Century(1731)=18.

Answer. 32 years; 1699 is in the 17th century and 1731 in the 18th century.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronological reasoning combines arithmetic with a naming convention; both should be applied explicitly.

Formal model. Integer arithmetic plus century function c(y)=floor((y−1)/100)+1.

Problem 810. Duration and centuries: 1763–1815

Knowledge context. Dates can be used as numbers, but historical labels such as centuries follow explicit conventions.

Given facts. An institution was founded in 1763 and reorganized in 1815. Use the rule: years 1–100 are the 1st century, 101–200 the 2nd, and so on. Duration is end year minus start year.

Rules. Apply the century rule mechanically; do not infer a century from the first two digits alone. Compute elapsed time by subtraction.

Task. How many years passed between the two events? In which centuries did 1763 and 1815 fall?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Elapsed time: 1815−1763=52 years. 2. Century(1763)=floor((1763−1)/100)+1=18. 3. Century(1815)=19.

Answer. 52 years; 1763 is in the 18th century and 1815 in the 19th century.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronological reasoning combines arithmetic with a naming convention; both should be applied explicitly.

Formal model. Integer arithmetic plus century function c(y)=floor((y−1)/100)+1.

H3. Sources and supported claims

Problem 811. What can one photograph prove?

Knowledge context. Historical sources are evidence, not automatic answers. The strength of a conclusion depends on what the source actually records.

Given facts. A historian has one source: a photograph. The source directly shows that a scene was photographed. A student proposes two claims: C1: a scene was photographed; C2: the whole population agreed with the ruler. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information.

Rules. A source supports only claims that can reasonably be inferred from what it contains. Absence of evidence for a broad claim is not proof of that claim. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies.

Task. Which claim is directly supported, and which is not justified by this source alone? Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain?

Step-by-step solution. 1. The photograph directly contains evidence for C1. 2. C2 is much broader and no stated feature of the source measures the opinion of the whole population. 3. Therefore C1 is supported and C2 is not established. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain.

Answer. C1 is supported. C2 is not justified by the source alone. Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports.

Knowledge takeaway. Good historical reasoning matches the scope of a claim to the scope of the evidence.

Formal model. Claim-evidence compatibility relation; accept only claims entailed by the source attributes.

Formal model. Claim-evidence compatibility relation; accept only claims entailed by the source attributes.

H4. Conflicting sources

Problem 816. Resolving conflicting sources: case 1

Knowledge context. Historical accounts can disagree. Reasoning requires evaluating how a source knows what it claims, not simply counting statements.

Given facts. Source A, written on the day of an event, says 40 carts arrived. Source B, copied 80 years later from an unknown account, says 90 carts arrived. Source C is an independent warehouse record from the same week and lists 42 carts. Cross-domain check: on a field sketch, 1 cm represents 3 km and two checkpoints are 6 cm apart.

Rules. When sources conflict, compare proximity to the event, independence, and whether a source has a reason or mechanism to record the specific fact. Agreement between independent relevant sources increases support but does not create absolute certainty. For the cross-domain check, real distance = sketch distance × kilometres per centimetre.

Task. Which account is better supported by the evidence given, and why? Cross-domain check: what real distance separates the checkpoints?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A is contemporary and reports 40. 2. C is an independent operational record and reports 42, close to A. 3. B is much later and has an unknown chain of transmission. 4. The cluster near 40–42 is therefore better supported than 90. Cross-domain check: 6×3=18 km.

Answer. An arrival count near 40–42 carts is better supported than 90. Cross-domain answer: 18 km.

Knowledge takeaway. Independent, relevant, well-positioned evidence usually deserves more weight than late repetition with unknown provenance.

Formal model. Evidence graph with source reliability/independence attributes; compare support for competing hypotheses.

Problem 817. Resolving conflicting sources: case 2

Knowledge context. Historical accounts can disagree. Reasoning requires evaluating how a source knows what it claims, not simply counting statements.

Given facts. Source A, an eyewitness diary, says the bridge opened on Monday. Source B, a later textbook, says Tuesday. Source C, an independent dated toll record, begins charging on Monday. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 8:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 83 map sheets and receives 8 additional sheets during the exercise.

Rules. When sources conflict, compare proximity to the event, independence, and whether a source has a reason or mechanism to record the specific fact. Agreement between independent relevant sources increases support but does not create absolute certainty. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Task. Which account is better supported by the evidence given, and why? Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

Step-by-step solution. 1. A and C are close to the event and independent. 2. Both point to Monday. 3. B is later and conflicts with two stronger, independent pieces of evidence. Cross-domain check: 8+2=10, so the team finishes at 10:00. Mixed-domain verification: 83+8=91.

Answer. Monday is better supported, while remaining a historical conclusion rather than absolute proof. Cross-domain answer: 10:00. Mixed-domain answer: 91 map sheets.

Knowledge takeaway. Independent, relevant, well-positioned evidence usually deserves more weight than late repetition with unknown provenance.

Formal model. Evidence graph with source reliability/independence attributes; compare support for competing hypotheses.

H5. Causes, conditions, and consequences

Problem 821. Cause-and-consequence chain: case 1

Knowledge context. Many explanations can be represented as condition-and-consequence rules. The logical form matters: necessary, sufficient, AND, and OR are not interchangeable.

Given facts. Facts: Rain occurred; The river was already high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning. Cross-domain check: a survey team starts work at 12:00 and works for 2 hour(s) without a break.

Rules. Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed. For the cross-domain check, finishing time = starting time + duration.

Task. Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule. Cross-domain check: at what time does the team finish?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rain and high river satisfy both conditions of the first rule. 2. Infer flooding. 3. Flooding implies road closure. 4. The working siren independently implies a warning. Cross-domain check: 12+2=14, so the team finishes at 14:00.

Answer. Flooding, road closure, and a warning can be deduced. Cross-domain answer: 14:00.

Knowledge takeaway. Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.

Formal model. Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

Problem 822. Cause-and-consequence chain: case 2

Knowledge context. Many explanations can be represented as condition-and-consequence rules. The logical form matters: necessary, sufficient, AND, and OR are not interchangeable.

Given facts. Facts: Rain occurred; The river was not high; The warning siren worked; The gate was closed. Rules: If rain occurs AND the river is already high, flooding occurs. If flooding occurs, the riverside road closes. If the siren works, residents receive a warning. Cross-domain check: a local committee has 11 members, requires at least 6 present for quorum, and 11 are present.

Rules. Use the rules exactly as written. AND requires all listed conditions; OR requires at least one. A one-way implication cannot automatically be reversed. For the cross-domain check, quorum exists when present members ≥ the stated threshold.

Task. Which consequences can be deduced by applying the rules exactly? Do not assume the converse of any rule. Cross-domain check: is quorum met?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Rain is true but the high-river condition is false. 2. The AND rule for flooding therefore does not fire. 3. Without flooding, road closure is not inferred. 4. The siren rule still gives a warning. Cross-domain check: compare 11 with 6; 11≥6 is true.

Answer. A warning can be deduced, but flooding and road closure cannot be deduced. Cross-domain answer: quorum is met.

Knowledge takeaway. Causal reasoning becomes clearer when every link is stated and the direction of implication is respected.

Formal model. Forward-chaining rule system over Boolean facts; apply implications until no new facts appear.

H6. Travel through time and space

Problem 826. Courier journey from Oak to Zephyr

Knowledge context. Historical travel can be analyzed with ordinary distance, speed, and time reasoning when the needed values are supplied.

Given facts. A courier leaves Oak for Zephyr at 7:00. Distance is 120 km and the stated average speed is 30 km/h. A council meeting in Zephyr begins at 10.0:00. Ignore stops and use travel time = distance ÷ speed.

Rules. Arrival time equals departure time plus travel time. To attend an event from its beginning, arrival must be no later than the event start.

Task. When does the courier arrive, and can the courier attend the meeting from its beginning?

Step-by-step solution. 1. Travel time=120÷30=4.0 hours. 2. Arrival=7.0+4.0=11.0. 3. Compare 11.0 with meeting time 10.0.

Answer. Arrival at about 11.0:00; no, the meeting has already begun.

Knowledge takeaway. Chronology and geography interact: being able to reach a place in time is a constraint, not a fact to memorize.

Formal model. Arithmetic time model; t_arrive=t_depart+d/v; compare with event time.
